newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - POST-56 HUNGARIANS: STRANGERS IN STRANGE LAND.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - POST-56 HUNGARIANS: STRANGERS IN STRANGE LAND.

text.p: Sebestyen Gorka says one of the strangest experiences of his life was carrying hunting rifles into Budapest airport in 1989 with his father Pal, imprisoned in Hungary during the 1950s for spying.

"I still remember arriving and seeing the expression on my dad's face after we picked up the luggage -- my father, an ex- political prisoner -- and both of us with guns on our backs and ammunition, being waved through customs," said Gorka, 26.
Pal Gorka, sentenced to life imprisonment after being betrayed, escaped during Hungary's 1956 uprising and settled in Britain.
Pal Gorka, 66, says he is sure he was betrayed by Kim Philby in 1950 because the British double agent ran resistance and information networks behind the Iron Curtain.
"We can't forget that several good Hungarians were executed," he added. "I was lucky that I escaped and I am still healthy."

Tens of thousands of Hungarians fled when the revolt against Soviet rule was crushed. Now some of their offspring, like Sebestyen Gorka, have returned, though such an idea seemed inconceivable until the collapse of communism in the late 1980s.

"My father once told me that maybe in my lifetime I would be allowed to visit Hungary once but he would certainly die in England. Now we both live here, and I work for the Ministry of Defence," said Gorka, who, with his father, went back to Hungary in 1989 for a hunting trip.

More than 250,000 people, many of them students and intellectuals, fled after the October uprising. Many settled in North America, Australia and Western Europe in one of the great refugee waves of the post-World War Two era.
"Students in vast numbers left the country," said historian Charles Gati, a senior vice president of the U.S. investment firm Interinvest.
"This was the worst emigration in Hungarian history," said Gati, who left in 1956. "The West got a group of promising people...while Hungary could not do well without young and talented people."
The children of emigres now travel freely to Hungary as tourists, for work or to find out if they feel "Hungarian". Some fit in easily, others find it more difficult.

"You find that you don't have the same experiences when you were growing up," said 27-year-old Spencer Jakab, who was born in the U.S., speaks Hungarian and is an investment analyst for CS First Boston brockerage in Budapest.

"I was watching 'The Brady Bunch' on television while Hungarians were in the Young Pioneers (the communist youth movement)," Jakab said. "There's no reason for me to feel like I have to make up for that, and it doesn't mean I can't live here and be happy."

Gorka, who works at an institute studying Hungary's possible future integration into NATO, said he was treated as an outsider until he told colleagues during an office party that he had served as a reservist in the British Territorial Army.

"You could see peoples' expressions change. It wasn't important for them that I came from another army from the wrong side, in the old terms," Gorka said. "The fact I was a soldier who knew what it was like to wear a uniform was the thing."
Piroshka Nagy, 33, whose parents both left in 1956 but met in America, says she is "a product of the revolution" -- and of its collapse.
"I wouldn't exist if it hadn't failed," said Nagy, who is married to a Hungarian librarian and works as a translator.
Nagy, mother of two children, said she moved to Hungary when she was 18 because "I always felt more Hungarian than American".
"But the strange twist of fate for me was that I've been feeling American ever since I had children...because that's sort of when your wholeness pops out in the open," Nagy said.
"I started realising, hey, there's a lot of stuff that is a part of me that I want to share with my kids, like speaking English."
Jozsef Nagy said he left at the age of 18 because he had fought Soviet soldiers, not out of ideological conviction but because "there is a gun, you can shoot. You never thought about it".
Today he is bitter that post-communist Hungary does not readily accept him.

"There's a lot of jealousy because they think we are all rich," said Nagy, 58, who retired as a building contractor in Britain after suffering several heart attacks. He says he has only a pension to live on following a separation from his wife.

"They think because we didn't go to jail and didn't eat bitter bread that we must have lived very well. But if I hadn't left I could have been educated. I lost more because I've been locked out for 39 years."
Nagy, like many exiles or "second generation" Hungarians born overseas, keeps a foot in both camps -- spending months at a time in Budapest but maintaining a home in Britain.
His ambivalence is shared by many, including Jakab who expects to return to the U.S. someday with his American wife.
"I love being here but I don't mind being in the U.S.," Jakab said. "For the sake of not having stress on our marriage I think we won't stay here forever.
"I'm lucky to feel comfortable in two societies." REUTER 150242 GMT oct 96
